subject: humanities
passage: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, builders in Bengal raised hundreds of brick temples whose walls are covered with terracotta panels showing epics, hunts, and daily life. Some scholars have read this tradition as a sign that Bengali patrons simply preferred fired clay to stone. Yet the wide river delta that makes up most of Bengal has abundant clay and almost no building stone, which had to be brought in at great cost. Art historian Rupa Sen found that in a western district where stone was quarried locally, temples built in the same period by the same communities were usually made of stone and decorated with carved stone panels. Sen's findings suggest that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: every temple built in Bengal during this period was made of brick and terracotta panels.
choices.B: terracotta in the delta mainly reflected the local materials, not a preference for clay.
choices.C: terracotta panels have lasted longer than carved stone panels in Bengal's humid climate.
choices.D: the stone temples were built by artisans who had never learned to work in terracotta.

explanation.why: Two facts combine. In the delta, stone was scarce and costly while clay was everywhere. Where stone was available locally, the same communities built in stone. If they had preferred clay, they would have used it even where stone was at hand. The terracotta tradition therefore seems to follow from available materials.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes stone temples in a western district, so not every temple was terracotta.
explanation.B: Correct. The same communities used stone where it was available, so terracotta in the delta most likely reflects the lack of stone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares how well the two materials have lasted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the stone temples were built by the same communities that built in terracotta.
